name: Kirkpatrick–Seidel output-sensitive convex hull
definition: For planar P with distinct x coordinates, construct upper chains U(S). If |S|≤2 return points in increasing x. Otherwise choose a strictly between the two central split coordinates, and let (u,v) be the upper supporting edge with u_x<a<v_x. Then U(S)=U({p∈S:p_x≤u_x}) concatenated with U({p∈S:p_x≥v_x}). Reflect y to obtain lower chain, reverse it and join without repeating extrema. To find the bridge, pair points p,q with p_x<q_x; K is the median pair slope k=(q_y−p_y)/(q_x−p_x). Let C=argmax_{p∈S}(p_y−K p_x) and u=min_x C,v=max_x C. If u_x<a<v_x return (u,v); if v_x<a discard the left member of pairs with k≥K; if u_x>a discard the right member of pairs with k≤K; retain all others and any unpaired point, then repeat. With two remaining points return them in increasing x.
variables: P input; S current subset; a split abscissa; n input size; h extreme vertex count; p,q paired points; k pair slope; K median slope; C support contacts; u,v bridge endpoints; U upper chain
assumptions: Finite planar coordinates with distinct x values and no three collinear; exact or robust slope, support and orientation comparisons. Choose the split between adjacent central order statistics, including for odd sizes; no input point is on the split. Empty and singleton inputs return directly
limitations: Worst-case O(n log h) arithmetic for h≥2 with worst-case linear selection for both median operations and linear partitioning; O(n) space with appropriate storage management. Sorting at each selection does not establish that bound. Duplicate abscissae and collinear triples are excluded here; arithmetic bit complexity and precision are separate
failure_conditions: Invalid general-position assumptions, unreliable support comparisons or a prune that loses the unique crossing bridge.
Nonshrinking candidate set or invalid split.
computation: Retain the odd unpaired point and apply the specified pair pruning only after testing extreme support contacts. Recursively compute the two surviving upper subchains. Repeat after reflecting y. Use linear-time order-statistic selection, not full sorting, to obtain the theoretical complexity.

source.citation: D. G. Kirkpatrick and R. Seidel (1986), The Ultimate Planar Convex Hull Algorithm?, SIAM Journal on Computing 15(1), 287–299, Algorithms 2.1 and 3.1 and Lemmas 3.2–3.3 reviewed in Stanford-hosted paper, pp. 289 and 292 page images reviewed. https://doi.org/10.1137/0215021 ; https://graphics.stanford.edu/courses/cs268-16-fall/Notes/KirkSeidel.pdf ; strict split and general-position restriction are catalogue conventions.

required_inputs: Finite planar points with distinct x values and no three collinear; robust exact comparisons and linear selection for the complexity claim.
mechanism_note: Output-sensitive alternative to Andrew, Graham and Jarvis for the same extreme hull objective. Support contact abscissae move left as slope increases; if all contacts are left of the split then K exceeds the bridge slope, so the left point of each pair of slope at least K cannot be a bridge endpoint (its partner would lie above the bridge). The right-contact case is symmetric. A constant fraction is eliminated up to rounding; the two hull subproblems each contain at most ceil(n/2) points. The theoretical bound is from the published algorithm, not measured runtime.

name: Pick lattice polygon area identity
definition: For a simple positive-area lattice polygon without holes, A=I+B/2−1 where I counts strict interior integer lattice points and B counts distinct boundary lattice points. For cyclic integer vertices p_i=(x_i,y_i), B=Σ_i gcd(|x_(i+1)−x_i|,|y_(i+1)−y_i|), using p_(n+1)=p_1.
variables: A unsigned Euclidean area; I strictly interior lattice count; B distinct boundary lattice count; p_i vertices; n vertex count; gcd greatest common divisor
assumptions: Simple closed polygonal boundary, positive area, integer Cartesian vertex coordinates, no holes and no zero-length edges; both clockwise and counterclockwise order permitted. Count each boundary lattice point once
limitations: Constant-time arithmetic given I and B; obtaining I by exhaustive bounding-box enumeration with an O(n) containment test costs O(nWH) where W and H are integer grid counts across the box. Computing B uses n gcd operations. Not applicable to arbitrary real-coordinate, self-intersecting or holed polygons as stated; exact integer arithmetic avoids overflow
failure_conditions: Noninteger vertices, invalid simple polygon, zero area, holes or incorrect lattice counts.
computation: For each edge with nonzero displacement (dx,dy), use gcd(|dx|,|dy|), counting its initial endpoint but not its terminal endpoint. Obtain I by a declared exact interior test or independent count. Evaluate 2A=2I+B−2 with integer arithmetic; compare against absolute doubled shoelace area when checking consistency.

source.citation: J. Harrison, A formal proof of Pick’s theorem, manuscript received 23 November 2015, statement and simple boundary assumptions reviewed (p. 1 page image and introduction), https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/~jrh13/papers/pick.pdf ; Algorithms for Competitive Programming, Pick’s Theorem – area of lattice polygons, statement cross-checked, https://cp-algorithms.com/geometry/picks-theorem.html ; boundary gcd formula independently derived.

required_inputs: Simple positive-area integer-lattice polygon and independently obtained interior and boundary counts.
mechanism_note: Lattice-area identity used as a diagnostic rather than a separate algorithm. Writing displacement as g times a primitive integer vector, Bezout’s identity implies that lattice locations on the closed edge occur at parameters j/g for j=0,…,g. A half-open edge contributes g locations, so summation counts boundary vertices once. Triangulating into empty lattice triangles yields unit half-area triangles; Euler incidence counting gives the identity. This does not certify polygon validity.
